Ronen Schaffer † † thanks: Denotes equal contribution. Hila Manor 1 1 footnotemark: 1 & Tomer Michaeli Affiliation: Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Email: {ronens@campus,hila.manor@campus,tomer.m@ee}.technion.ac.il Abstract Transformers are widely assumed to exhibit token-decoding explainability. In particular, in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers, decoding individual patch tokens has become a common diagnostic tool due to its tendency to yield human‑interpretable outputs. In light of the increasing popularity of this approach, an important question is whether token‑decoding explainability is an inherent property of transformers that should be expected to hold across architectures, scales, and training objectives, or merely an artifact of some implicit bias. In this paper we systematically study token‑decoding explainability across diverse ViT settings, spanning architectures, scales, and training objectives, using both controlled experiments and real-world models. We find that while some models indeed exhibit aligned and interpretable token decodings, others exhibit either inverted explainability maps or a complete lack of correlation with the image semantics. As we show, these tendencies toward different explainability behaviors are not intrinsic to the architecture and can vary arbitrarily with changes in the optimization landscape. We provide theoretical support for these observations by demonstrating a setting where a single fixed toy transformer architecture can provably implement the optimal classification rule in multiple ways, which differ in their patch-decoding explainability patterns. Our results show that token‑decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers, but rather an outcome contingent on the problem setting and thus should not be a-priori assumed to hold. Code can be found in our project website . 1 Introduction Transformers ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , originally presented in the context of natural language processing, have proven powerful across various domains, including images, audio, and video ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Gong et al., 2021 ; Arnab et al., 2021 ; Yun et al., 2019 ) , achieving state-of-the-art performance on countless tasks ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Kirillov et al., 2020 ; Zheng et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2019 ) . Following their growth in popularity, significant attention has been devoted to mechanistically understanding their internal representations. One of the simplest methods for explainability in transformer language models is Logit Lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) . This cornerstone approach interprets each intermediate hidden state of the model by projecting it back into the model’s vocabulary space. This is done by multiplying the token’s embedding by the unembedding matrix, which is normally applied only to the tokens of the final layer. Logit Lens has been widely adopted for exposing the evolution of predictions across layers in large language models (LLMs) ( Pal et al., 2023 ; Prakash and Lee, 2023 ; Wendler et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Patil et al., 2024 ; Wang, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , and inspired numerous derivative approaches for decoding intermediate tokens ( Belrose et al., 2023 ; Din et al., 2024 ; Sakarvadia et al., 2023 ) . It has also expanded to other domains, including images ( Joseph et al., 2025 ; Neo et al., 2025 ) , audio ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Glazer et al., 2026 ) , and video ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . In light of the widespread adoption of these techniques, it seem natural to ask whether we can universally trust the validity of patch-token decoding explainability. Much of the current literature assumes that intermediate representations consistently map directly to interpretable concepts ( Joseph et al., 2025 ; Vilas et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Neo et al., 2025 ) . For instance, it is commonly expected that when interpreting the classification result of a vision transformer (ViT) on an input image of an elephant, the patch-tokens corresponding to the spatial location of the elephant would exhibit a higher logit for the “elephant” class than to any other class. This is illustrated in Fig. 1 , which shows a map of the “elephant” logit across all patch tokens of the image. Several recent works noted that this might not always be the case, observing that in some transformers token-decoding maps can look inverted ( Li et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2025 ; Bousselham et al., 2024 ) . Yet, these observations have been treated as a localized effect to be engineered away. In this paper, we show that there is no guarantee that transformers exhibit token-decoding explainability. We begin by analyzing dozens of pre-trained ViTs, showing they break the common assumption of aligned -explainability. Instead, many models exhibit either inverted -explainability or completely unexplainable intermediate representations. For example, when applying patch-token decoding explainability techniques to prominent contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) , the explainability maps are typically inverted. Next, through a series of controlled synthetic experiments, we expose how different conditions cause the same architecture to change its explainability behavior. We observe that different tasks and data distributions induce implicit biases toward different explainability regimes. Those biases do not deterministically determine the explainability behavior, however they control the probability of a training run to converge to either an aligned- or an inverted-explainability solution. Finally, we prove that aligned-explainability cannot be an inherent property of all transformers. Specifically, we present a simple classification task for which the optimal classification rule admits an implementation by a toy, single layer transformer architecture in infinitely many ways. We prove that among the sets of weights that implement the optimal solution, some correspond to an aligned-explainable model and some to an inverted-explainable model. Our findings demonstrate that the behavior and explainability of decoded representations can vary widely depending on the optimization landscape, from the task, to the training loss, and even the data distribution itself. This implies that token-decoding explainability is not a fundamental property of transformers, but merely a fragile byproduct of their training conditions. As such, when training a transformer on a new task, it cannot be a-priori assumed that zero-shot decoding of its internal states would reveal any meaningful or localized information about the semantics encoded in those tokens. Here, the elephant is aligned and the cat is inverted. 2 Related work Explainability techniques for ViTs. Explainability methods broadly fall into two families. The first attributes the ViT’s prediction to the input image patches. Early techniques aggregated attention across layers for standard transformers ( Abnar and Zuidema, 2020 ) and were subsequently adapted to ViTs ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) . Later methods propagated relevance through self-attention in both vision and language models ( Chefer et al., 2021b ; Ali et al., 2022 ; Achtibat et al., 2024 ) . Other approaches rely on gradient-based weighting of attention maps or features ( Chefer et al., 2021a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . However, most attribution techniques are computationally intensive, requiring, e.g . , heavy backward passes to compute gradients. The second family maps intermediate tokens directly into the model’s output space. Logit Lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) popularized this idea, decoding intermediate LLM hidden states with the final unembedding matrix. Tuned Lens ( Belrose et al., 2023 ) refined this by training per-layer translators to correct depth-wise affine drift. Given its simplicity and gradient-free nature, zero-shot token-decoding became popular for LLM explainability ( Pal et al., 2023 ; Prakash and Lee, 2023 ; Wendler et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024b ; Patil et al., 2024 ; Wang, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) and was quickly adopted for ViTs by applying the classification head to decode patch tokens ( Vilas et al., 2023 ; Joseph et al., 2025 ) . Since then, it has been extended to multimodal language models ( Neo et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) , video models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , and audio models ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Glazer et al., 2026 ) . Yet, unlike LLM decoders where unembeddings naturally decode individual tokens, ViT encoder heads are trained only on the class-token. Despite this divergence, zero-shot patch decoding is assumed to reliably yield aligned maps. Here, we show this is highly model-dependent and not guaranteed. Patch misalignment in CLIP. Several previous works observed that CLIP’s token decoding can be misleading. Li et al. (2023) identified an “opposite visualization” effect where patch similarity maps highlight the background complement. Similar negative contrast was subsequently reported in open-vocabulary segmentation and dense inference ( Zhou et al., 2022 ; Bousselham et al., 2024 ; Lan et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , and analyzed geometrically by Kang et al. (2025) . However, since prior art focused on downstream dense prediction, they largely approached this from an interventionist perspective, developing test-time remedies like attention surgery or feature pruning to force spatial alignment. Rather than treating inversion as an isolated engineering flaw to be patched, we study it through the lens of representation underdetermination and ask whether alignment should be expected in the first place. By systematically analyzing contrastive models across architectures, objectives, and scales, we show that inverted-explainability is a pervasive implicit bias of zero-shot patch decoding in VLMs, which can be shaped by the data in controlled settings. 3 Explainability of vision transformers 3.1 Definitions Consider an image I I of an object located inside a spatial mask ℳ {\mathcal{M}} . The image is given as input to a ViT with N N patch-tokens and one class-token. Let { T ​ [ I ] i } i = 1 N \smash{\{T[I]_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}} denote the patch tokens in some layer within the ViT. A common approach to interpreting these tokens is to treat each of them as if it were the class token at the final layer. Crucially, this zero-shot approach examines native representations, rather than training auxiliary probes. For example, in ViTs for classification, we can apply to each of these tokens the classification head, which is normally applied only to the class-token of the last layer. We can then inspect the logit value corresponding to the true object class, 𝒞 {\mathcal{C}} , and treat it as the patch’s score 𝒮 {\mathcal{S}} . Similarly, in image encoders of contrastive VLMs like CLIP, we can apply the projection head to each patch token and compute its cosine similarity with the text embedding of a template sentence of the form “ a photo of a 𝒞 {\mathcal{C}} ” obtained from the text encoder. This provides a score 𝒮 {\mathcal{S}} for each patch. The map of scores obtained for all patches in a given layer is often assumed to visualize how the model interprets each spatial location of the image, as shown in Fig. 1 . To quantitatively measure the quality of an explainability map for image I I , we calculate the average score of the object’s tokens, 𝒮 obj {\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{obj}} , and the average score of the background tokens, 𝒮 bg {\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{bg}} , as 𝒮 obj ​ [ I ] = 1 | ℳ | ​ ∑ j ∈ ℳ 𝒮 ⁡ ( T ​ [ I ] j ) , 𝒮 bg ​ [ I ] = 1 | ℳ c | ​ ∑ j ∉ ℳ 𝒮 ⁡ ( T ​ [ I ] j ) , {\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{obj}}[I]= rac{1}{|{\mathcal{M}}|}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{M}}}{\mathcal{S}}(T[I]_{j}),\quad{\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{bg}}[I]= rac{1}{|{\mathcal{M}}^{c}|}\sum_{j

The relation between these two mean scores can be used to define the explainability behavior for that image. The common interpretation is that if 𝒮 obj > 𝒮 bg {\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{obj}}>{\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{bg}} (green triangle in Fig. 1 ) then the object patches better correlate with the object’s label than the background tokens, meaning the object tokens are directly aligned with the expected classification. However, if 𝒮 bg > 𝒮 obj {\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{bg}}>{\mathcal{S}}_{	extnormal{obj}} (blue triangle in Fig. 1 ), the background tokens have higher scores than the object tokens, which according to the common interpretation means the model’s knowledge of the class is localized in opposition to the object’s tokens. Explainability analysis can be applied to any layer. However, for conciseness, all experiments use the following convention unless specified otherwise. For models in which the patch tokens of the last layer were not affected by the loss during training, we always use the layer before the last. This includes, e.g . , most ViT classifiers, in which the classification head operates only on the class token at the last layer, so that the patch tokens of that layer are not affected by the loss during training. For models in which the last layer’s patch tokens are affected by the loss, we always show the last layer. This includes, e.g . , DINOv2, whose pretrained classification head expects as input the class token concatenated to the mean of the last layer’s patch tokens. Further details are in Apps.
